strengths: The part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) is a well-motivated and timely representation: the paper convincingly argues that object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions are too coarse to specify support/contact geometry, and the two-level node structure (object nodes with part nodes carrying labeled surfaces) is a concrete, sensible formalization of part-aware relations.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is a coherent, well-explained pipeline (coarse localization → part-level alignment → pose sampling with a priori guarantee of constraint satisfaction → Sapien simulation refinement), and the DAG/unique-supporter design gives a principled assembly order that makes the constraint problem tractable.

PARSE-10K is a substantial resource contribution: 10,000 scenes across 17 room types with part segmentation, physics optimization, and part-level contact annotations (Table 1 shows this combination is not offered by prior datasets), which plausibly fills a real gap for physics-grounded spatial supervision.

The evaluation spans both spatial understanding (three tasks, strong baselines including GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus-4, Robobrain2.0, Qwen3-VL) and scene generation, and the grounding-agnostic metric is a thoughtful analysis that separates relational reasoning from visual grounding.
Limitations are candidly discussed (manual PAG construction sensitivity to canonical poses, near-parallel contact assumptions), which aids scientific assessment.
weaknesses: The VLM fine-tuning evaluation has a serious distribution confound: the fine-tuned model is trained on rendered PARSE-10K scenes and evaluated predominantly on the same rendered distribution, so 97.4% / 86.2% accuracy versus zero-shot commercial VLMs likely reflects in-distribution fitting rather than general spatial intelligence gains. Real COCO images are mentioned as added to the test set, but no separate results on the real-image subset are reported, leaving the generalization claim unsupported.

The scene generation comparison is weak on quantitative evidence: no objective metrics (e.g., contact accuracy, collision rates, FID/KID, physics success rate) are reported—only qualitative figures and a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes each). Moreover, the baseline (InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT) differs from the proposed model in both method and training data, so observed gains cannot be attributed to PAG conditioning versus dataset differences; a same-data ablation baseline is missing.

The solver itself—the core technical contribution—is never quantitatively evaluated. There are no statistics on success rate, constraint satisfaction, runtime, or failure modes, making it hard to verify the claims of 'high success rate' and 'avoiding costly cycles of blind rejection sampling'.

The pipeline for extracting PAGs from real images is described only at a high level ('extracting layout priors from real images'); there is no detail on how PAGs are obtained or validated, no statistics on PAG relation types, and no quality assessment of the extracted layouts, which weakens reproducibility of the dataset construction.

The unique-supporter DAG assumption excludes common configurations (objects resting on two supports, leaning against walls plus floor), limiting representational generality; the impact of this restriction on dataset diversity is not quantified.

Missing details undermine reproducibility: fine-tuning hyperparameters and diffusion training details are deferred to a supplementary not provided here; no statement about public release of code or the dataset is verifiable from the manuscript.
The user study's preferred-scene protocol (choose one of three per criterion) and small sample size (20 raters) give limited statistical power; no variance or significance analysis is reported.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated: object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions are genuinely too coarse to specify support, containment, and contact regions, and the proposed Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) with two-level nodes and labeled part surfaces is a concrete, sensible formalization of part-level relations for scene synthesis.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is a reasonable engineering contribution: progressive constraint contraction over a DAG-ordered assembly, with a priori satisfaction of geometric relations before final pose sampling, avoids blind rejection sampling and is a defensible design choice.

PARSE-10K fills a real gap in the data landscape. Table 1 credibly positions it as the only large-scale indoor scene dataset combining physical simulation, part annotations, and part-level contact annotations, with competitive scale (10K scenes, ~50 objects/scene, 132 categories).

The experimental scope covers two distinct downstream uses (VLM spatial reasoning fine-tuning and graph-conditioned scene generation), demonstrating breadth of applicability, and the grounding-agnostic metric in Sec. 5.1 is a thoughtful control to separate relational reasoning from visual grounding gains.

The paper is generally well-written and organized, with clear illustrations (Figs. 2-3) of the representation and solver behavior, and honestly acknowledges limitations (manual PAG construction, canonical-pose sensitivity, near-parallel contact assumption).
weaknesses: The spatial-reasoning evaluation risks distribution contamination: the fine-tuned model is tested on MCQs rendered from PARSE-10K scenes, i.e., the same synthetic rendering distribution and asset/vocabulary used in training. Distractors are generated by 'randomly replacing object and relation labels', which tends to produce easy negatives and can inflate accuracy (97.4% on Visual Relation MCQ). The COCO real-image generalization test is mentioned but no separate quantitative results for it are reported, leaving generalization claims unsupported.

The central claim that part-level supervision specifically drives the gains is not isolated. 'Ours' is a Qwen3-VL fine-tuned on PARSE-10K compared against zero-shot generalist VLMs; a controlled baseline (e.g., fine-tuning on an object-level scene-graph dataset of comparable size) is absent, so improvements could stem from fine-tuning volume, domain match, or synthetic-image statistics rather than part-level annotation.

The scene-generation comparison is confounded: PARSE-10K-trained model is compared to InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT, so dataset differences (object count, asset quality, contact density) and method differences are entangled. No quantitative generation metrics are provided—only a user study with 20 participants evaluating 12 scenes, which is too small to support claims like 'consistently preferred' without significance analysis; nor are physics-stability or contact-fidelity metrics measured automatically despite the framework's emphasis on physical validity.

The DAG/unique-supporter constraint is presented as 'the necessary mathematical structure', but it limits expressiveness for common configurations with multiple simultaneous supports (e.g., a plank resting on two boxes, objects in mutual contact). The representational cost of this choice is not analyzed or quantified.

Key technical details needed for reproducibility and rigor are missing from the main paper: there are no formal constraint equations for the solver (e.g., how coplanarity/contact constraints are parameterized), no statistics on solver success rates, failure modes, or simulation stabilization frequency, and the pipeline for extracting layout priors from real images to build PAGs is described only at a high level. The acknowledgment that PAG construction is 'partially manual' raises questions about annotation consistency and quality control that are not addressed.

The evaluation of the solver itself is absent: no comparison against alternative layout solvers (e.g., constraint optimizers used by Holodeck/LayoutVLM-style systems) to substantiate the claimed efficiency and geometric-fidelity advantages over procedural/LLM-based approaches discussed in Sec. 2.

strengths: The core idea of modeling inter-object relations at the part level (PAG) is well-motivated and addresses a genuine representational gap: object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions cannot specify contact/support regions, and the paper clearly articulates this (e.g., the 'book on a table' spine-vs-cover ambiguity in Sec. 1).

PARSE-10K appears to be a uniquely annotated resource: 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories, with part-level contact graphs obtained from physical simulation (COACD convex decomposition + Sapien simulation + surface-point contact detection, Sec. C.1). Table 1 shows no existing dataset combines physics optimization, part annotations, and part-level contact annotations.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is technically coherent: coarse-to-fine constraint accumulation (object-level half-space constraints, then part-level surface alignment), final rejection-sampled pose validation, and a final physics refinement pass. The claim that constraint accumulation avoids blind rejection sampling is reasonable, and Algorithm 1 plus the relation dictionary (Tab. 4) make the method concrete and reproducible.

Downstream utility is demonstrated along two axes: fine-tuning Qwen3-VL yields large gains on visual relation MCQ (97.4 vs 86.2 for base Qwen3-VL), part-level contact MCQ (86.2), and scene graph generation (F1 76.6 vs 33.2), and the diffusion-based scene generation model trained on PARSE-10K produces denser, more contact-rich scenes than InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT.

Limitations are candidly acknowledged (partially manual PAG construction, sensitivity to canonical poses), and the supplementary material is unusually detailed (full algorithm, hyperparameters, prompts, simulation parameters), supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The VLM comparison (Tab. 2) is confounded: a LoRA fine-tuned Qwen3-VL is compared against zero-shot generalist VLMs on tasks drawn from PARSE-10K's own distribution. The claimed advantage therefore conflates dataset value with in-distribution fine-tuning; a fairer baseline would be fine-tuning the same base model on an alternative dataset (e.g., 3D-FRONT-derived supervision). The grounding-agnostic metric is described but no numbers are actually reported for it, so the claim that gains stem from 'stronger relational understanding' rather than grounding is not fully substantiated.

The scene generation evaluation is thin: no quantitative metrics (e.g., FID/KID, object count, contact accuracy, physical validity rates) are reported—only a 12-scene user study with 20 participants. Moreover, comparing 'our model trained on PARSE-10K' against InstructScene trained on 3D-FRONT confounds model and dataset (3D-FRONT averages only 6.9 objects/scene vs 49.9); notably, 'Ours(uncond)' scores *lower* than InstructScene on realism (27.5% vs 33.8%), which suggests the comparison is driven by dataset characteristics rather than method.

Diversity of the dataset may be overstated: all 10,000 scenes derive from only 200 manually designed PAG templates (Sec. C.2) via a custom UI. The distributional diversity of layouts is bounded by these templates, and the paper provides no analysis of how much scene-to-scene variation the solver actually introduces beyond asset/scale sampling.

Annotation quality is only partially verified: assets outside PartNeXt are generated with Rodin, auto-segmented with P3-SAM, and semantically labeled by GPT, with only 'manual verification of canonical pose'—not of the part segmentation or labels themselves. Contact labels rely on a 1mm threshold on convex-hull point sampling, which may produce noisy contacts; no human audit of label accuracy is reported.

Solver robustness is not quantified: failure cases (empty constraint intersections, exceeded MaxTrials) are mentioned but no success/failure rates, assembly-time statistics, or sensitivity to relation-dictionary coverage are given, making it hard to judge how general the framework is beyond the 200 curated templates.
No explicit commitment to releasing the dataset, code, or PAG editing UI is stated in the main text, which limits reproducibility of what is primarily a dataset/infrastructure contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: part-level geometric relations resolve the inherent ambiguity of object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions (e.g., the 'book on a table' spine-vs-cover example), and the paper operationalizes this concretely in the Part-centric Assembly Graph (PAG) with a two-level node structure, dual-granularity edges, and a DAG/unique-supporter assembly constraint.

The Part-Aware Spatial Configuration Solver is technically well developed: coarse-to-fine progressive constraint contraction (Algorithm 1, Table 4 relation dictionary) converts prepositions into geometric constraints over labeled part surfaces, avoiding costly rejection sampling; the supplementary material provides enough detail (surface resolution, Sapien refinement, COACD-based contact extraction) for reproducibility.

PARSE-10K is a genuinely new resource: 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories, ~50 objects/scene, and part-level contact graphs. Table 1 shows no existing dataset offers both part annotations and part-level contact annotations at this scale, and the gallery/statistics (density >1.35 obj/m2 in 55% of scenes; >57% of scenes with >50 part contacts) support the claim of contact-rich complexity.

Broad downstream validation covering both spatial understanding (fine-tuning Qwen3-VL on three tasks with strong gains, e.g., 97.4% visual relation MCQ, 76.6/78.2 SGG F1) and generative modeling (PAG-conditioned diffusion), demonstrating the representation is useful beyond dataset construction.
Limitations are honestly stated in the conclusion, including the partially manual PAG construction and sensitivity to canonical poses.
weaknesses: Evaluation of the fine-tuned VLM is largely in-domain: test scenes are rendered from the same procedural generation pipeline as the training data, and strong baselines (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude) are evaluated zero-shot against a model fine-tuned on that distribution. The COCO real-image additions are mentioned but no separate quantitative results are reported for them, so claims of generalization to real images and 'stronger relational understanding' (as opposed to domain adaptation to synthetic rendering styles and distractor patterns) are not fully substantiated.

The scene generation comparison is comparatively weak: only one baseline (InstructScene), only qualitative figures, and a small user study (20 participants, 12 scenes). No standard quantitative generation metrics (e.g., FID/KID, object count statistics, contact-accuracy measures against ground truth) are reported, and notably the unconditioned model trained on PARSE-10K is rated *below* the 3D-FRONT baseline on realism (27.5% vs 33.8%) and contact fidelity (26.3% vs 28.8%), which weakens the claim that PARSE-10K alone improves generation; the benefit appears contingent on PAG conditioning.

Dataset diversity may be overstated: 10,000 scenes are driven by only 200 manually designed PAG templates across 17 room types, so structural diversity is bounded by the templates; the 'real-image guided' label (Table 1) should be interpreted with this in mind. Additionally, no explicit statement is given in the main text about public release of the dataset, code, and benchmarks, which matters for a resource paper.

The DAG and unique-supporter assumptions limit the class of expressible scenes (e.g., mutually supporting objects, circular support structures), but the paper does not quantify how often these cases occur or how the solver handles relation conflicts beyond flagging failure cases.

Possible shortcut-learning risk in the MCQ tasks: distractors are generated by randomly replacing object/relation/part labels from predefined vocabularies, so accuracy gains may partly reflect learning of distractor statistics; no human or ablation analysis on distractor difficulty is provided.

Writing is generally clear but somewhat repetitive in the results sections (paragraphs restating Table 2 results), and some claims such as 'guaranteed a priori to satisfy all non-collision-related relations' deserve more careful qualification (e.g., multi-directional ray-cast enclosure thresholds).
